title: Pattern: Long-Running Tasks
summary: Accept work fast, run it on a durable queue with idempotent workers, heartbeated leases, bounded retries and a DLQ, and tell the client when it is done.
body:
Some work cannot finish inside an HTTP request: transcoding a video, generating a 500-page report, running a user's code against 100 test cases, or provisioning infrastructure. Load balancers and clients time out around 30 to 60 seconds, deploys kill in-flight requests, and holding a thread per slow job caps throughput. The pattern is to accept the request quickly, hand the work to a durable queue, and let workers process it while the client checks back. It shows up in video pipelines, online judges, crawlers, exports and any "we'll email you when it's ready" feature.

## Draw the sync/async boundary

Decide what the user must wait for and what they must not. Validation, authorization and durably recording the request are synchronous. The expensive part is asynchronous. The API returns `202 Accepted` with a job ID within milliseconds, and the job record becomes the contract between the user and the system.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"POST /jobs"| API["API service"]
    API -->|"insert queued"| DB[("Job table")]
    API -->|"enqueue jobId"| Q[["Job queue"]]
    Q --> W1["Worker"]
    Q --> W2["Worker"]
    W1 -->|"status, progress, result key"| DB
    W2 -->|"status, progress, result key"| DB
    W1 -->|"output"| S[("Blob store")]
    C -->|"GET /jobs/id"| API
    Q -.->|"failed too often"| DLQ[["Dead-letter queue"]]
```

The API writes a job row (`queued`) and enqueues the job ID. Workers pull from the queue, update the row to `running`, write outputs to a blob store, and finish with `succeeded` or `failed`. The client reads status from the job table, not from the queue. Messages that keep failing are moved to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for inspection instead of being retried forever.

Writing the row and enqueueing are two separate systems, so a crash between them leaves a row with no message. Fix this with a transactional outbox (write the row and an outbox record in one transaction, then relay to the queue) or by having a sweeper re-enqueue jobs stuck in `queued` past a deadline. Also include an idempotency key on `POST /jobs` so a client retry after a timeout does not create a second job.

## The job record

A useful job table has: `job_id`, `owner_id`, `type`, `status` (`queued`, `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `cancelled`), `attempt`, `progress`, `lease_owner`, `lease_expires_at`, `result_ref`, `error`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, and the idempotency key with a unique constraint. Results larger than a few kilobytes belong in blob storage with a reference in the row.

## Delivery, leases and retries

Most queues give **at-least-once** delivery. When a worker receives a message it becomes invisible to other consumers for a **visibility timeout** (SQS) or is held as unacknowledged (RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub). If the worker acknowledges, the message is deleted; if it crashes, the timeout lapses and another worker gets it. Two consequences follow:

1. **Duplicates happen**, so job processing must be idempotent. Write outputs to deterministic keys (`results/{jobId}`), and make the final status transition conditional (`UPDATE jobs SET status='succeeded' WHERE job_id=? AND status='running' AND lease_owner=?`).
2. **Long jobs need heartbeats.** Rather than a one-hour timeout that delays recovery from crashes by an hour, use a short lease (say 60 seconds) and have the worker extend it every 20 seconds. A stalled worker stops heartbeating and the job is reclaimed quickly.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Queue
    participant W as Worker A
    participant DB as Job table
    participant W2 as Worker B
    Q->>W: deliver job 42 (invisible 60s)
    W->>DB: status=running, lease until t+60
    loop every 20s
        W->>Q: extend visibility
        W->>DB: extend lease, progress
    end
    Note over W: worker crashes
    Q->>W2: redeliver job 42 after timeout
    W2->>DB: attempt=2, take lease
    W2->>DB: status=succeeded (conditional on lease)
    W2->>Q: ack
```

Worker A heartbeats while healthy; after it dies the message reappears and Worker B takes over with a new attempt number. The conditional update on lease ownership stops a zombie Worker A, if it comes back, from overwriting B's result.

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and classify errors. A transient error (timeout, throttling) is retried; a permanent one (invalid input, a corrupt file) fails immediately. After a maximum number of attempts (3 to 5 is typical), the job goes to the DLQ and the row is marked `failed` with the error. A DLQ needs an owner, an alert and a redrive tool, or it is just a place where work silently dies.

## Telling the client

| Mechanism | How it works | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polling | Client calls `GET /jobs/{id}` every few seconds, backing off | Default; simple, cache-friendly, works everywhere |
| Long polling or SSE | Server holds a connection and pushes status changes | Interactive UIs that show progress bars |
| WebSocket | Bidirectional channel already used by the app | Apps that already maintain a socket |
| Webhook | Server POSTs to a customer URL on completion | Server-to-server APIs; sign payloads and retry deliveries |
| Email or push notification | Out-of-band message | Jobs measured in minutes to hours |

Polling 1 million active jobs every 5 seconds is 200,000 reads per second, so either back off (1s, 2s, 5s, 10s), serve status from a cache, or switch to push for interactive cases.

## Priorities, fairness and scaling

One FIFO queue lets a single tenant who submits 50,000 jobs starve everyone else. Common remedies: separate queues per priority class with dedicated or weighted worker pools; per-tenant concurrency limits enforced when a worker claims a job; and separate queues for very different job sizes so a 2-hour transcode does not block 2-second thumbnails.

Autoscale workers on **queue depth and age of the oldest message**, not CPU. If each job takes 30 seconds and you want backlog cleared within 5 minutes, then workers needed is roughly backlog multiplied by 30 and divided by 300; a backlog of 10,000 needs about 1,000 workers. Set a ceiling so a burst cannot exhaust a downstream database, and scale in gently because terminating a worker mid-job wastes work.

## Cancellation

Cancellation is cooperative. `POST /jobs/{id}/cancel` sets `cancel_requested=true` (or status `cancelling`). A queued job is skipped when a worker picks it up; a running worker checks the flag at each heartbeat or checkpoint and stops cleanly, releasing resources. Do not promise instant cancellation of side effects that have already happened, such as an email already sent.

## Failure modes and common mistakes

- Doing the work inside the request with a longer timeout. It fails on deploys, retries and proxies.
- Treating the queue as the status store. Queues are not queryable by job ID; keep a job table.
- Assuming exactly-once delivery, so a retried job charges a card twice or emits two emails.
- One giant visibility timeout instead of heartbeats, so crashed jobs stall for an hour.
- No DLQ, or a DLQ nobody watches.
- Scaling workers on CPU when they are mostly waiting on I/O, so the backlog grows while CPU looks idle.
- Poison messages: a job that crashes the worker process every time. Count attempts before processing, not after.

## How to use it in an interview

Name the boundary ("submission is synchronous and durable; execution is asynchronous"), draw the API, job table, queue and workers, then volunteer the guarantees: at-least-once with idempotent workers, heartbeated leases, bounded retries into a DLQ. Numbers that matter: job duration distribution, arrival rate and therefore worker count (arrival rate multiplied by average duration, by Little's law), and polling load. Expect follow-ups on worker crashes mid-job, duplicates, noisy tenants, cancellation and how the user learns the result.

## Interview exercise

Design "export my account data" for a service with 50 million users, where exports take 1 to 40 minutes and produce up to 20 GB of files. Specify the API, job states, how you avoid two concurrent exports for one user, how a worker crash at minute 35 is handled, and how the user receives the download.

keyTakeaways: Make submission synchronous and durable (job row plus idempotency key, return 202) and execution asynchronous.
Keep job status in a queryable table; the queue is a delivery mechanism, not a status store.
Queues deliver at least once, so workers must be idempotent and final status writes conditional on lease ownership.
Use short leases extended by heartbeats instead of one huge visibility timeout so crashed jobs recover quickly.
Autoscale on queue depth and oldest-message age, and isolate priorities and tenants so one burst cannot starve others.
